questions.stem: A 26-year-old man presented with worsening headache, chills, fevers, and neck stiffness. He had no significant past medical history. He smoked 1 pack per day (PPD), and drank 2–3 beers every day. He reported unprotected sex with multiple male partners (around 5–6 partners in last 1 year). He lived in Phoenix, Arizona. He worked for a commercial painting company and had recently finished cleaning and painting an overpass. On examination, his temperature was 39.4°C, pulse 110 beats/minute, blood pressure of 98/58 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/minute. He was saturating 95% on room air. A lumbar puncture was performed after a neuroimaging. Investigations: CT head: no acute process or space-occupying lesions LP opening pressure 40 cmH2O CSF white cell count 40/ μL (30% polymorphonuclear cells and 70% mononuclear cells) CSF glucose 30 mg/dL CSF protein:70 mg/dL Blood cultures negative at 24 hours
questions.lead_in: What diagnostic test should be performed to allow appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: CSF cryptococcal antigen His clinical presentation is consistent with meningitis. He has high-risk sexual behavior that increases probability of HIV . High opening pressure with predominantly mononuclear cells and normal CT imaging raise concern for possible cryptococcal meningitis with undiagnosed HIV . CSF cryptococcal antigen, which is highly specific and sensitive for cryptococcal meningitis, should be performed to establish the diagnosis. A normal CT and no encephalopathy make HSV less likely. Epidemiology is concerning for CNS coccidioidomycosis, but the high opening pressure is more suggestive for cryptococcosis. Additionally the definitive test in patients with presumed HIV would be CSF antigen for coccidioidomycosis, not the antibody. Syphilis is always a possibility, especially in patients with high-risk sexual behavior, and should be ruled out. However, this case presentation is unlikely to be due to syphilis, and the VDRL alone has a low sensitivity. Histoplasmosis is possible due to his exposure (cleaning and painting the old bridge will involve exposure to aerosolized bird droppings), however he is outside of the endemic area, and meningitis with a high opening pressure would be a rare presentation of the disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q3

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man presented with fevers, headaches, and altered mental status. He lived in Tucson, Arizona, and worked for a landscape management company. He was known to have HIV , atrial fibrillation, and hypertension but was not taking ART . Investigations: MRI brain: hydrocephalus and meningeal enhancement seen CD4 count 95 cells/μL HIV viral load undetectable CSF microscopy: lymphocytic pleocytosis CSF complement fixation IgG serology for Coccidioides positive 1:32 The patient was treated with IV fluconazole and intrathecal amphotericin B for 2 weeks with improvement in symptoms and MRI findings. The patient was then transitioned to oral fluconazole 400 mg daily upon discharge.
questions.lead_in: What duration of antifungal therapy should be recommended?
questions.explanation: Indefinite Due to high relapse rates in meningeal and CNS coccidioidomycosis in HIV patients, secondary prophylaxis with oral azole therapy is recommended indefinitely, regardless of CD4 count recovery.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q36

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman presented with new onset speech disturbance, confusion, and left arm weakness. Her friend said that she had reported being unwell for 10 days with a mild headache and fever. She had been born and brought up in the Philippines. She was normally fit and well and was awaiting occupational health clearance to start work as a hospital nurse. A lumbar puncture was performed after a CT head and clotting were checked. Investigations: Peripheral white blood cell count 6.2 ×109/L HIV Ag/Ab negative CSF white cell count 655 ×106/L; 99% lymphocytes CSF protein 2910 mg/L CSF/plasma glucose 1.2/5.6 mmol/L CSF microscopy: no organisms seen A working diagnosis of TB meningitis (TBM) was made, and she was started on quadruple antituberculous therapy and dexamethasone.
questions.lead_in: What agent is the most critical at the start of TBM treatment?
questions.explanation: Isoniazid Isoniazid has excellent CSF penetration (90%–95%) and has early potent bactericidal efficacy. Rifampin penetrates the CSF less well, but its importance has been demonstrated in the higher mortality of rifampin-resistant TB infections. There is no conclusive evidence that pyrazinamide improves outcomes of TBM, but it has good CSF penetration. There is also little evidence to support which fourth drug to use. Both streptomycin and ethambutol have poor CSF penetration and can have significant adverse reactions.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q12

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presented with headache, fevers, and altered mental status. Her husband reported that she had been unwell 2 weeks earlier with fevers and dry cough which resolved spontaneously. She had returned 3 weeks ago from a 4-week trip to New Mexico. She normally lived in Chicago. She had no significant past medical history. She denied smoking and drank alcohol occasionally. She lived on a farm with 2 dogs and 10 chickens. On examination, her temperature was 38.4°C, pulse 90 beats/ min, blood pressure of 88/58 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min with SPO2 95% on room air (RA). Her CT head showed no acute process or space-occupying lesions. Investigations: Lumbar puncture showed: Opening pressure 18 cmH2O CSF white cell count 60/μL (20% polymorphonuclear cells, 80% mononuclear cells) CSF glucose 20 mg/dL CSF protein 90 mg/dL Blood cultures negative HIV Ag/Ab negative
questions.lead_in: What test is most likely to be diagnostic?
questions.explanation: CSF coccidioidal antibodies Endemic exposure (travel), biphasic presentation with initial respiratory illness that resolves spontaneously followed by dissemination to extrapulmonary sites (brain/bone/skin) raises suspicion for coccidioidal meningitis. Considered to have high specificity and sensitivity in coccidioidal meningitis, CSF coccidioidomycosis serologies should be performed to establish the diagnosis. Cryptococcosis is less likely considering normal opening pressure and absence of underlying immune condition. Some patients with Cryptococcus are immunonormal, but that is more common with Coccidioides. Blastomycosis can have similar presentation with dissemination, but CNS involvement is usually with brain abscess, not meningitis. Histoplasmosis rarely affects the CSF .
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q2

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presented with fluctuating headaches that had slowly worsened over the preceding month. He had lost 8 kg in weight and thought he had been having some hot flushes. His wife reported that he had started intravenous biological treatment for arthritis 3 months earlier, but she was unsure what it was. He had not recently travelled. He had been born and brought up in the UK but had spent several years working in southern Africa in his twenties. On examination he was mildly confused. His GCS was 14/15. His temperature was 37.9°C. There was neck stiffness but no purpura. There was no focal neurology. A CT head and lumbar puncture were performed. Investigations: CT head – no space-occupying lesions. Normal appearances of ventricles and brain parenchyma. CSF white cell count 641 ×106/L; 99% lymphocytes CSF protein 1614 mg/L CSF/plasma glucose 1.4/4.8 mmol/L CSF microscopy: no organisms seen HIV Ag/Ab negative He was started on presumptive antituberculous therapy and high-dose steroids and clinically began to improve.
questions.lead_in: What biological agent is most likely to lead to infection with tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Infliximab Infliximab is a chimeric mAb directed against TNF . All biologics targeting TNF- α carry a risk of reactivation of tuberculosis. The risk is higher with infliximab and adalimumab than with etanercept. Most cases are likely to be due to reactivation of LTBI, but newly acquired infection is responsible for a number of cases in areas of low TB prevalence. Screening for LTBI should be done before initiating therapy with anti-TNF agents. Abatacept prevents CD28 binding, inhibiting T-cell costimulation. It carries an increased risk of severe infection but not opportunistic infections or TB. Alemtuzumab (otherwise known as Campath) carries a risk for Pneumocystis jirovecii ( carinii) pneumonia (PCP), herpes, and CMV infections. Natalizumab blocks binding of VLa4 on VCAM1, reducing migration of activated white cells. It is associated with a risk of JC virus infection leading to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Rituximab is a B cell-depleting monoclonal anti-CD20 antibody and requires consideration of HBV reactivation, prophylaxis for PCP , and JC virus infection leading to PML.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q4

questions.question: Tuberculous meningitis and latent TB management.

parts.text: For TB meningitis, list 6 drugs in the initial regimen and name the 2 cranial nerve palsies most commonly involved.
What is the preferred regimen for children with latent TB, and (in adults, other than isoniazid for 9 months) what are 2 acceptable regimens for LTBI?
Name 2 rapid diagnostic modalities/tests that help make the diagnosis.

parts_raw.text: 6 drugs for TB meningitis, what are the 2 cranial nerve palsies are most commonly involved?
Preferred regimen for kids with latent TB? (in adults, other than INH x9mos, what are 2 acceptable regimens for LTBI)
2 rapid diagnostic modalities/tests that you can do to help your dx?

questions.model_answer:
a) Six drugs: (1) isoniazid (2) rifampin (3) pyrazinamide (4) ethambutol (5) adjunctive corticosteroid, e.g. dexamethasone/prednisone (recommended for CNS TB) (6) pyridoxine (vitamin B6) given with INH. Most commonly affected cranial nerves: cranial nerve VI (abducens) most often, then cranial nerve III (oculomotor).
b) Children: 9 months of isoniazid (300 mg daily) is the recommended regimen for LTBI in children (and adults). Two acceptable adult alternatives to 9 months INH: (1) 3 months of once-weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (DOT); (2) 4 months of daily rifampin (10 mg/kg, max 600 mg). [3 months daily INH + RIF is also acceptable.]
c) Two rapid tests: (1) nucleic acid amplification / GeneXpert MTB/RIF (Ultra) on CSF; (2) AFB smear of centrifuged sediment from large-volume CSF obtained by repeated lumbar punctures (yield rises to ~90% with 4 large-volume LPs). CSF PCR is positive in roughly 60-90% of culture-confirmed cases.
questions.beyond_mandell: The text does not name the specific cranial nerves; CN VI > CN III is established teaching (Mandell/standard neurology).

questions.model_answer:
a) Bacterial causes (Table 88.2): (1) Mycobacterium tuberculosis (most common cause of chronic meningitis; immigrant from endemic Nepal at risk of reactivation). (2) Treponema pallidum (neurosyphilis). (3) Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme). (4) Tropheryma whipplei (Whipple disease); others include Nocardia, Actinomyces, Brucella.
b) Fungal causes (Table 88.2): (1) Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii (most common fungal cause). (2) Coccidioides. (3) Histoplasma; others Candida, Sporothrix, Blastomyces.
c) Parasitic causes (Table 88.2): (1) Taenia solium (neurocysticercosis). (2) Angiostrongylus cantonensis (eosinophilic meningitis). (3) Acanthamoeba / Balamuthia (granulomatous amebic meningoencephalitis).

cohort_answer.text:
A) Mycobacterium TB, Listeria monocytogenes (incubation 11-90 days, mean 31 days), Borrelia burgdorferi (no Lyme in Australia though), Treponema pallidum, Tropheryma whipplei, Nocardia spp (abscess), Brucella spp, Burkholderia pseudomallei (rare but found in this region).

B) Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Sporothrix schenckii, Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii, Talaromyces marneffei, Coccidioides immitis (if travel to Arizona, California).

C) Taenia solium (Neurocysticercosis), Angiostrongylus cantonensis (eosinophilic meningitis, rat lung worm), Acanthamoeba (Granulomatous Amebic Encephalitis), Toxoplasma gondii, Baylisascaris procyonis (if child or cognitive impairment), Gnathostomiasis species, Schistosoma spp (if in Africa/SE Asia).

questions.model_answer:
a) Enterovirus (summer/early-autumn seasonality; in contrast to HSV, enteroviral CNS disease is markedly seasonal).
b) (1) HSV-2 (the commonest herpesvirus cause of aseptic meningitis, typically with primary genital infection); (2) varicella-zoster virus; (3) mumps virus.
c) Diagnosis: Mollaret meningitis — benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis, episodes lasting 3–7 days and resolving without neurologic sequelae, of which HSV-2 is responsible for most cases. Confirm with HSV DNA detection by PCR on CSF (far more sensitive than CSF viral culture and now the mainstay of diagnosis); expect a lymphocytic pleocytosis (10–1000 cells/mm3), normal/near-normal glucose and mildly elevated protein. Prophylactic acyclovir is often offered for frequent recurrences.
questions.beyond_mandell: VZV and mumps as aseptic meningitis causes are from other Mandell chapters, not this one.

cohort_answer.text:

questions.question: For each of the following, indicate whether you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): tuberculous meningitis; neurocysticercosis with a viable intraparenchymal cyst; cerebral malaria; acute schistosomiasis; a large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR.
questions.question_raw: For each of the following, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): TB meningitis; Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst; Cerebral malaria; Acute schistosomiasis; Large echinococcal cyst with risk of rupture during PAIR.

parts.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario with rationale.

parts_raw.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario and rationale

questions.model_answer: (1) TB meningitis: YES - adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in confirmed TBM (not HIV+, where evidence is weaker). Note: steroids are NOT routine during purely empirical/diagnostic therapy as they blunt the clinical and CSF response and can worsen an undiagnosed fungal infection. (2) Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst: YES - corticosteroids control the peri-lesional inflammation/edema provoked by antiparasitic (albendazole) therapy; not indicated for calcified cysts with isolated edema. (3) Cerebral malaria: NO - randomized data show steroids are harmful (prolonged coma, more complications). (4) Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama / acute neuroschistosomiasis): YES - corticosteroids given with praziquantel to suppress the hypersensitivity reaction. (5) Large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR: NO - no role for adjunctive steroids; risk is anaphylaxis, managed with antihistamines/epinephrine and peri-procedural albendazole, not steroids.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the TB-meningitis point is touched in this chapter (p. 1225, advising against routine steroids during empirical therapy). Steroid use in confirmed TBM, neurocysticercosis, cerebral malaria, schistosomiasis, and echinococcosis/PAIR rests on IDSA/WHO guidance and the respective Mandell disease chapters, not the chronic meningitis chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Katayama fever (acute schisto) - yes (5 days pred 40mg followed by praziquantel per Mandell's). Neurocysticercosis intraventricular lesions not calcified and no hydrocephalus - yes (dexamethasone 6-8mg/day divided TID for 28 days, then slow taper over 2-8 weeks; not indicated in calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema; steroids lower praziquantel levels and increase albendazole levels, partial reason for albendazole use in limited CNS disease). TB meningitis - yes (non-HIV TB pericarditis can also use steroids, not for pleural; if HIV+ insufficient evidence). Ruptured echinococcus - no (not addressed in guidelines or UpToDate). Cerebral malaria - no

questions.model_answer:
a) TB meningitis: Yes (adjunctive corticosteroids reduce mortality; ATS/IDSA/WHO).
b) Neurocysticercosis with a viable intraparenchymal cyst: Yes, co-administered with antiparasitic therapy to blunt the inflammatory reaction (IDSA/ASTMH NCC guidelines); not indicated for calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema.
c) Cerebral malaria: No (corticosteroids are associated with worse outcomes/prolonged coma; contraindicated).
d) Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome/neuroschistosomiasis): Yes (corticosteroids before/with praziquantel; CDC/UpToDate).
e) Large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR: No (risk of anaphylaxis is managed with peri-procedural antihistamines and anaphylaxis readiness plus concomitant albendazole, not adjunctive steroids).
questions.beyond_mandell: These topics (TB meningitis, neurocysticercosis, cerebral malaria, schistosomiasis, echinococcosis) are outside the Acute Meningitis chapter; answers rest on IDSA/ASTMH, WHO malaria, and CDC parasitic-disease guidance.

cohort_answer.text: TB meningitis - Yes, TB standards. Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst - Yes, NCC guidelines. Cerebral malaria - No, associated with worse outcomes. Acute schistosomiasis - Yes, UTD/CDC. Also consider with neuroschistosomiasis. Large echinococcal cyst with risk of rupture during PAIR - No (no resources mention this). Additional notes: katayama fever (acute shisto) - yes (5 days of pred 40mg, followed by praziquantel per Mandell's); neurocysticercosis intraventricular lesions not calcified and no hydrocephalus - yes, dexamethasone 6-8mg/day divided TID for 28 days then slow taper over 2-8 weeks; not indicated in calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema; steroids lower praziquantel levels and increase albendazole levels; TB meningitis - yes; non-HIV TB pericarditis can use steroids (not for pleural; if HIV+ insufficient evidence); ruptured echinococcus - no; cerebral malaria - no
